summary: A humorous essay on creation myths and origin stories across cultures, from cosmic eggs and world-bearing animals to divine families, primal chaos, creation by sound, and serpents. It mixes folklore (Nut and Geb, Ymir, the Rig Veda, Ouroboros) with quoted commentary from various figures in autumn 2023, and compares ancient myths to the Big Bang and to social media as a modern 'chaos'. It concludes that playful retellings reflect a need to connect with our past and our enduring fascination with beginnings.
one_line: A comedic survey of world creation myths, from cosmic eggs and serpents to the Big Bang, tying ancient storytelling to modern social media culture.
key_facts: Professor Olga Schmidt of the University of Arcane and Mythological Studies (UAMS) began a project cataloging the different ways the world could have been created.

On October 31, 2023, Olga Schmidt joked that existence was as likely to be a cosmic sneeze as any other theory, and said she prefers the story of a celestial cow licking salt for a thousand years to free the earth.
The 'World on the Back of a Giant Creature' genre of creation narrative ranges from turtles to elephants to cosmic whales.
Fictional anthropologist Timmy Thatcherson said in a podcast released September 20, 2023 that ancestors were like a pre-literature George R.R. Martin by a Neolithic campfire.
Twitter user @Egghead2048 asked on September 21, 2023, 'What came first, the cosmic egg or the cosmic chicken?'
In ancient Egyptian myth the sky goddess Nut is romantically involved with the earth god Geb; in Norse myth the world is made from the body of a dismembered giant named Ymir.
Laura Winklevoss, a novelist and self-proclaimed myth-revivalist, said on November 13, 2023 that these stories 'put soap operas to shame'.

Many origin stories begin with chaos or a formless void separating into cosmic order, as in the ancient Greek, Chinese and several Indigenous traditions; Schmidt calls it 'the kitchen sink before the dishwasher of the gods gets to work'.

The Christian Bible's 'Let there be light' and the Rig Veda's 'One' who breathed without air suggest sound or the word precedes creation; D.J. BeatBoots said on December 1, 2023 the universe may have started with 'a sick beat drop'.
On November 7, 2023, an Ouroboros meme captioned 'When you're so hungry you could eat the world' became the unofficial sign-off for creationism conversations on social media.
Amateur astronomer Cindy Harper wrote in a September 15, 2023 blog post that the Big Bang has less personality than a world-bearing tortoise but 'a lot more fireworks'.
Social critic Ollie Quinn said during the viral Tweetstorm of 2023, 'Today's gods wear sneakers and have YouTube channels.'
